title: Diarrhea in the field: what to do
asks: how do I treat diarrhea in the backcountry
bad diarrhea what do I do
got the runs from creek water
diarrhea how long does it last
blood in diarrhea what does it mean
what to drink and eat with diarrhea
diarhea for two days and feel weak
kid has diarrhea and wont drink
the trots on trail what helps
answer: The danger of diarrhea is dehydration, which can become severe rapidly. Put the emphasis on fluid support and rehydration: oral rehydration (replacing the lost fluid by drinking) is the keystone treatment.
Oral rehydration solution (ORS), which contains water, sugar and salt, is the preferred drink: infectious diarrhea loses 2 to 3 times more electrolytes (body salts) than sweating.

Replace the fluids and salts lost through diarrhea and vomiting. With profuse watery diarrhea (as in cholera), encourage the person to drink as much ORS as possible: more than the total volume lost. Even a person who is vomiting can be rehydrated with ORS taken in frequent small sips, as long as they are fully alert and able to swallow without choking.
Signs that rehydration is succeeding: regular urination (every 3 to 4 hours), and urine color approaching light yellow (straw).

Rest. Give a liquid or low-residue diet that includes broths containing salts. Breads, raisins, rice, apples and tea are often helpful if the person can tolerate food. Avoid milk products: this is the HHS ship's manual's advice, written for adult crew. Keep breastfeeding a baby: CDC says breastfeeding is the safest way to feed an infant during emergencies.
Acetaminophen may be given for headache or fever.
Most traveler's diarrhea resolves within 3 to 5 days.
Protect others: wash hands regularly, and a person with diarrhea should not prepare food until fully recovered.
warnings: Children: not feeding well, or not being able to drink or breastfeed, is a danger sign in a child. So are vomiting everything, unusual sleepiness or confusion, moving only when stimulated, and convulsions. A child with any of these needs URGENT medical attention (WHO).
Children become dehydrated more rapidly than adults. Infants and young children are particularly at risk.
Give drinks only to a person who is fully alert and able to swallow without choking. For anyone else, get medical help: severe cases may need fluids into a vein (IV).

Get medical help for severe diarrhea or diarrhea containing blood or mucus (dysentery): it can be incapacitating, and some forms are life threatening without medical care and IV rehydration. Diarrhea with blood may require specific antibiotic therapy.

Get medical advice for any diarrhea that causes serious acute symptoms or lasts more than a week or two, and whenever there is any question about hydration, mental state, or lack of response to treatment. Most people can be treated with ORS by mouth, but severe cases may require fluids into a vein (intravenous therapy).
Dehydration leading to coma or death may occur when extreme diarrhea is combined with vomiting or fever.

Avoid medicines that slow the gut, such as over-the-counter or prescription anti-diarrheal medications, unless advised medically otherwise: they keep the infection in the gut and can make it longer and more severe.
A large amount of watery, "rice-water" stool suggests cholera, which can rapidly cause severe dehydration and shock: start rehydration immediately and get medical advice promptly.
Black, dark or reddish stool can suggest bleeding in the stomach or intestines.

quotes.text: Diarrhea occurs commonly during military deployments and may produce gastrointestinal (stomach and bowel) body water losses of 1 to 2 quarts per day. Although most "traveler's diarrhea" resolves within 3 to 5 days, it can exacerbate dehydration due to sweat losses – particularly in hot environments. Oral rehydration is the keystone treatment. More severe diarrhea (for example, dysentery, or severe diarrhea containing blood or mucus) can be incapacitating and some forms even life threatening in the absence of medical intervention and IV rehydration.
Dehydration stemming from infectious diarrhea results in electrolyte losses 2 to 3 times greater than from sweating. Therefore, ORS is the preferred beverage for treating diarrheal dehydration.

When managing these patients, emphasis should be placed on fluid support and rehydration. Dehydration leading to coma or death may occur when extreme diarrhea is combined with vomiting or fever. This will cause a loss of water taken in and of water stored by the body. Severe dehydration may occur rapidly.

Oral replacement should attempt to replace both fluids and electrolytes lost in the dehydration process. Sodium and glucose transport are coupled in the small intestines because the presence of glucose stimulates the intestinal absorption of water and solutes. For this reason, oral rehydration solutions should contain water, sugar and salt.

The basic principle of rehydration therapy is to replace the fluids and salts that are lost through diarrhea and vomiting. This means giving a lot of ORS. The amount of ORS needed varies, depending on the severity of the dehydration and the amount of ongoing fluid losses. Patients need to drink more ORS than the total volume of fluid lost through diarrhea and vomiting. Patients should have ORS constantly available at the bedside and should be encouraged to drink as much as possible. Even patients with vomiting can be rehydrated with ORS taken in frequent small sips. An indication that rehydration therapy is succeeding is regular urination (every 3 to 4 hours).

Rehydration fluids are to be given to the otherwise healthy patient until: the patient can maintain normal urine output levels of 50-100 ml/hour for an adult. the urine color approaches a light yellow (straw) color

Treatment of diarrheal disease is directed towards supportive care. The patient should be placed on bed rest and made as comfortable as possible. A liquid or lowresidue diet should be given that includes soft drinks and broths containing salts. A "BRAT" (breads, raisins, rice, apples, tea) diet is often helpful if the patient can tolerate foods. Milk products should be avoided as the intestinal lining often is denuded and lacking the enzymes necessary to metabolize them.

Diarrhea with blood or white blood cells in it may require specific antibiotic therapy. Fluid replacement by itself will greatly reduce the discomfort level for the patient and relieve the dizziness experienced when standing. Acetaminophen may be given for headache or fever.

Basic medical advice should be sought by radio for any diarrheal illness that causes serious acute symptoms or persists for more than a week or two. Advice should also be sought if there is any question regarding hydration status, mentation, or lack of response to therapy. Agents that slow gut motility, such as over-the-counter or prescription anti-diarrheal medications, should be avoided unless advised medically otherwise. They cause the infectious agent to be retained in the gut and can lengthen the infection and increase its severity.

The most important aspect of treatment for cholera is replacing the lost fluids rapidly by way of rehydration therapy. Most patients can be treated with oral rehydration salt (ORS) solutions. Severe cases may require intravenous therapy.

Patients with the symptoms of cholera should immediately receive treatment, as described below, without waiting for a physician or laboratory to confirm the diagnosis. Medical advice should also be obtained promptly by radio.

Many diseases are transmitted by the oral fecal route. Hands are often contaminated when urinating or defecating. This contamination can spread disease to the individual and to the entire crew. REGULAR HANDWASHING BY EVERY CREW MEMBER is critical to the health of the entire crew.
Persons with diarrhea, vomiting, or open sores on their hands should not prepare food until they have fully recovered;

Check stool: Any significant diarrhoea can cause dehydration. A large amount of watery, "rice-water" stool suggests cholera, which can rapidly cause severe dehydration and shock. Black, dark, or reddish colored stool can suggest stomach or intestinal bleeding.

Children have a relatively larger surface area (compared to their body volume) and are thus likely to become dehydrated more rapidly. Infants and young children are particularly at risk as they are unable to say when they are thirsty and cannot drink more on their own.

Children with danger signs need URGENT attention and referral/ handover to a provider able to provide advanced paediatric care. Paediatric danger signs include: • Signs of airway obstruction (stridor or drooling/unable to swallow saliva) • Increased breathing effort (fast breathing, nasal flaring, grunting, chest indrawing or retractions) • Cyanosis (blue colour of the skin, especially at the lips and fingertips) • Altered mental status (including lethargy or unusual sleepiness, confusion, disorientation) • Moves only when stimulated or no movement at all (AVPU other than “A”) • Not feeding well or cannot drink or breastfeed • Vomiting everything • Seizures/convulsions • Low body temperature (hypothermia)
Oral fluids work well for most dehydrated patients who are not obtunded and can take fluids without risk of aspiration or vomiting.
Breastfeeding is the safest way to feed an infant during emergencies. For infants who are not breastfeeding or being fed breast milk, ready-to-feed infant formula is the next safest option.

conflict: ORS RECIPE (this card gives no recipe; it belongs to the oral-rehydration-solution card): TB MED 507 (2022) gives 6 level teaspoons of table sugar and ½ level teaspoon of table salt in 1 quart of potable water; HHS Ship's Medicine Chest 2003 gives 1½ tablespoons of sugar, ½ teaspoon of table salt, ¾ teaspoon of baking soda and ¼ teaspoon of salt substitute per liter or quart, or one ORS packet in one liter of clean (boiled) water. FOOD (the card follows Ship's Medicine Chest): Ship's Medicine Chest says a liquid or low-residue diet with salted broths and soft drinks, BRAT foods if tolerated, no milk products, and (cholera section) resume a normal diet as soon as able; ATP 3-50.21 (2018) survival table says limit intake to fluids only for 24 hours. HOME REMEDIES (left out): ATP 3-50.21 gives strong tea every two hours and a chalk, charcoal or dried-bone mixture as extreme-measure remedies; no other kit source supports them, and Ship's Medicine Chest says to avoid anti-diarrheal agents. The ORS-volume, small-sips and urination lines come from the Ship's Medicine Chest cholera section. FEMA P-2064 (2020) has nothing on diarrhea. CHILD WHO WILL NOT DRINK (warning added in revision): the kit's only text is WHO BEC's general paediatric danger signs ('Not feeding well or cannot drink or breastfeed', 'Vomiting everything', altered mental status, 'Moves only when stimulated', convulsions; 'Children with danger signs need URGENT attention'). It is a general list for sick children, not written about diarrhea. ORAL FLUIDS ONLY IF ALERT (limit added in revision): no kit document says in so many words not to give ORS by mouth to a drowsy person with diarrhea; the limit restates TB MED 507's sentence on oral fluids ('not obtunded and can take fluids without risk of aspiration or vomiting'), which is written about heat casualties, as the oral-rehydration-solution card does. That sentence also says 'or vomiting', while HHS says 'Even patients with vomiting can be rehydrated with ORS taken in frequent small sips'; the card keeps HHS's small sips for a vomiting person who is alert. BREASTFEEDING (added in revision): no kit document discusses breastfeeding during diarrhea. HHS's 'Milk products should be avoided' is in a book written for adult ship's crew; CDC Use Safe Water During an Emergency (2024) says 'Breastfeeding is the safest way to feed an infant during emergencies'; WHO BEC treats a child who cannot breastfeed as a danger sign. The card keeps HHS's advice, labelled as written for adults, and says to keep breastfeeding; owner to confirm.

review.notes: Re-review 2026-11-25 (claude-opus-5-5 xhigh). All three previous findings fixed: W1 adds WHO BEC's paediatric danger signs (cannot drink or breastfeed, vomiting everything, unusual sleepiness or confusion, moves only when stimulated, convulsions; URGENT attention), attributed; A3 and W3 limit drinking to a person fully alert and able to swallow, from TB MED 507's oral-fluids sentence, and conflict says that sentence is about heat casualties and that its 'or vomiting' differs from HHS's small sips; A5 labels the no-milk advice as HHS's, written for adult crew, and says keep breastfeeding, attributed to CDC, with conflict noting the kit has no text on breastfeeding during diarrhea. Checked in context: TB MED 507 diarrhea and ORS paragraphs; HHS gastroenteritis, cholera and hygiene text; WHO BEC stool and child text; CDC. No kit source recommends anti-diarrheal drugs (HHS lists loperamide in its medicine chest only), so W7 hides no conflict. All asks answered; kind fact acceptable; no PDF junk. Optional: W7 could name loperamide as an example. previous review: (verdict fail, by claude-opus-5-5 (xhigh), independent review 2026-11-24) Problems (point d): (1) The card claims 'kid has diarrhea and wont drink' but never says what to do. WHO BEC paediatric danger signs: 'Children with danger signs need URGENT attention and referral' and the list includes 'Not feeding well or cannot drink or breastfeed', 'Vomiting everything' and lethargy. Fix: add a warning that a child (or anyone) who cannot or will not drink, keeps vomiting everything, or is drowsy needs urgent medical care, with that quote. (2) A3 'Even a person who is vomiting can be rehydrated with ORS taken in frequent small sips' has no 'awake and able to drink' limit (same issue as the ORS card). TB MED 507 5-3: oral fluids for patients 'who are not obtunded and can take fluids without risk of aspiration'. (3) A5 'Avoid milk products' comes from HHS's adult crew text; a parent may stop breast milk. The kit says 'Breastfeeding is the safest way to feed an infant during emergencies' (CDC Use Safe Water). Fix: 'Avoid milk products (adults); keep breastfeeding babies.' Confirmed: TB MED 507 diarrhea and ORS paragraphs; HHS gastroenteritis, cholera and hygiene text (supportive care, BRAT, avoid anti-motility agents, seek advice criteria, severe cases may need IV, rice-water stool); WHO stool and children text. Food and recipe disagreements listed. kind 'fact' is acceptable (a set of measures). No PDF junk. Minor: HHS's medicine list names loperamide; W4 could name it as an example of an anti-diarrheal to avoid.
